query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with an ultrathin, conformal nickel interlayer (using atomic layer deposition) will improve the wettability between tungsten and copper, thereby suppressing phase separation and interfacial void formation during high-temperature consolidation and under subsequent irradiation. This should lead to significantly enhanced thermal conductivity in the composite, relative to the untreated W–Cu composite under service conditions relevant to plasma-facing joint applications.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite containing discrete tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix (akin to chemically plated W–Cu composites prepared by conventional sintering or SPS routes).
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step, ultrathin (~5 nm) nickel coating on tungsten particle surfaces via atomic layer deposition (ALD) prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: Processing via high-temperature sintering (near or above the copper melting point, e.g., ~1350 °C) or rapid SPS conditions in a controlled atmosphere, followed by exposure to high heat flux and irradiation conditions representative of plasma-facing component joints (simulated irradiation with appropriate keV ions).
generation.structural_mediator: The conformal nickel interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
generation.mechanism: The Ni coating improves the wettability of tungsten by copper, promoting uniform copper melt infiltration and reducing the interfacial energy mismatch. This enhanced interfacial bonding mitigates copper evaporation and void formation during high-temperature processing. Under irradiation, the interlayer is expected to stabilize the interface against radiation-induced segregation and void nucleation, maintaining a continuous copper network for effective electron and heat transport.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ALD-Ni coated composite will show a more homogeneous microstructure with fewer or smaller interfacial voids, reduced phase separation, and improved densification. Consequently, thermal conductivity is predicted to be significantly higher (by an estimated direction of >20% improvement relative to uncoated samples, with the exact value subject to experimental determination) under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite processed under similar sintering and irradiation conditions, which typically exhibits phase separation with interfacial void formation leading to lower thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to composites processed under high-temperature sintering or SPS conditions and is targeted at service environments where high thermal flux and irradiation are present (e.g., joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components). Its effectiveness may be limited if the processing temperatures or irradiation doses exceed the stability range of the Ni interlayer.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies have shown that higher sintering temperatures improve copper network formation (PMC12028711::web::017) and that additives like Cu@Gr can enhance interfacial bonding (PMC5736653::web::011), none have directly targeted both phase separation and void formation with a dedicated interfacial metallic coating. The current proposal extends these findings to explore whether an ALD Ni interlayer can simultaneously improve wetting and irradiation stability—there remains uncertainty on the long-term behavior of the Ni layer under extreme irradiation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites under identical processing conditions, one with ALD-deposited ~5 nm Ni coatings on tungsten particles and one without any coating. Process both via the same high-temperature sintering or SPS route. Subject samples from each set to simulated service conditions including high heat flux and controlled irradiation (e.g., with Ar+, He+, or D+ ions at fluences comparable to plasma-facing joint conditions).
measurements: Microstructural analysis (using SEM/EDS and TEM) for quantification of interfacial void density and phase homogeneity.
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via laser flash analysis) before and after irradiation.
Interfacial bonding quality assessment (e.g., via nanoindentation or microhardness tests) along the W–Cu interfaces.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in interfacial voids and phase separation, or if thermal conductivity improvements are not observed (i.e., they are comparable to or worse than those of the uncoated samples) after high-temperature consolidation and irradiation exposure, then the hypothesis is falsified.
